rationale: The source gives the recursive higher-derivative and C^k conventions. The item repackages them for an arbitrary interval, includes the library's one-sided endpoint convention, declares C^0 explicitly, and records the nesting C^{k+1} subset C^k.

The sources state the nth product rule with the same binomial sum and differentiability hypothesis. The repository changes notation only. Its induction through Pascal's rule was audited as a local proof rather than an identifiable transcription of either source proof.

The source states the same higher-order Rolle theorem: continuity on the closed interval, n differentiability in the interior, n+1 ordered zeros, and a zero of the nth derivative between the extreme zeros. The numbered iterative proof is local.

Both sources state that the derivative of a differentiable real function on an interval has the intermediate value property, with the same quantifiers and direction. The extremum-based numbered proof is local.

The sources explain that a derivative has Darboux's property and hence cannot have a jump, while giving the standard oscillatory derivative discontinuity. The item translates this into the library's removable/jump/essential classification; the removable case is the same local intermediate-value obstruction.
The peer-reviewed source states the same theorem that an injective real function on an interval with the Darboux property is strictly monotone. The repository's order-trichotomy proof is local.

The literature supplies the three exact ingredients: derivatives have the Darboux property, injective Darboux functions are strictly monotone, and a monotone function on an interval with interval image is continuous. The item packages them into the injective-or-monotone derivative corollary.

The sources state Cauchy's mean value theorem in quotient form under continuity, differentiability, and nonvanishing g', including the necessary conclusion g(b) not equal to g(a). The short derivation is local.

The sources give the 0/0 rule under the same derivative-quotient and nonvanishing-denominator-derivative hypotheses. The item uniformly packages one-sided, two-sided, infinite-endpoint, and extended-real limits and derives infinity by t=1/x, so it is a convention-rich semantic restatement rather than an exact copy.

The sources give the infinity-over-infinity rule for finite and infinite endpoints. The item consolidates endpoint modes, extended-real derivative limits, absolute divergence, and eventual fixed signs in the library's conventions. Its Cauchy-mean-value proof is local.

The source defines the degree-n Taylor polynomial and pointwise remainder with the same coefficients. The item adapts it to the library's canonical-natural and finite-sum notation and explicitly permits any point where the required derivatives exist.
The source states that the Taylor polynomial matches every derivative of f through order n at the centre. This is the same claim and range of orders; the termwise finite-sum calculation is local.

The source gives the Schlomilch/Roche remainder formula with the same parameter and interpolating point. The item restricts the parameter to an integer between 1 and n+1, states relative-interval regularity explicitly, and uses the library's factorial and integer-power conventions.

The sources give the Lagrange and Cauchy forms as the corresponding special cases of Taylor's remainder. The item packages both in one corollary under its parent theorem's relative-interval conventions.

The live Taylor's theorem article states the Peano conclusion under k-times differentiability at the expansion point. The published item assumes the stronger condition of k-times differentiability on an open neighbourhood and separately records n=0, so it is a valid specialization rather than an exact transcription; the inductive quotient proof is local.

The live Taylor's theorem article states the Lagrange remainder formula under the corresponding derivative hypotheses and the resulting uniform error estimate. This matches the item's bound M|x-a|^{n+1}/(n+1)!; the repository proof is a direct local application of its preceding remainder theorem.

The source gives the same pointwise second-derivative test: f'(c)=0 with positive or negative f''(c) yields a strict local minimum or maximum. The item proves it through derivative monotonicity under the same weak pointwise hypothesis.

The source gives the higher-derivative test with the parity and sign alternatives. The item replaces a neighbourhood C^n hypothesis by the sharper Peano-at-the-point hypothesis and spells out the odd case's increase-through-the-point conclusion.

This is a repository-specific scope statement about the exact conventions and deliberate omissions of the current page, not an established mathematical proposition. Alpha checked each cross-reference and omission directly against current disk and repaired the injective/monotone derivative-continuity sentence with its exact page theorem and declared dependency.

The literature states that a zero second derivative is inconclusive and gives the higher-derivative test that distinguishes the three outcomes. The item combines the standard witnesses x^4, -x^4, and x^3 into one explicit refutation.

The normalized quartic Hermite cell 16u^2(1-u)^2, its periodic gluing, and the chosen derivative values are a bespoke local construction. Direct polynomial differentiation gives matching value and first derivative at every seam, periodicity and boundedness are immediate from the fractional-part definition, and substituting the displayed quarter-points gives derivative values 3 and -3.

The witness x^2 psi(1/x) uses the preceding bespoke polynomial oscillator rather than the classical trigonometric example. The difference quotient at zero is bounded by |x| times a fixed bound for psi, while the product/chain calculation and the oscillator's recurring derivative values directly show discontinuity of F' at zero.

The family x^k|x| being C^k but not C^{k+1} is a standard elementary smoothness example, and the item's piecewise derivative computation verifies it. A real literature search found the k=2 instance in MIT 18.100B notes but no allowed source stating the full quantified family, so this row requires Alpha's independent established-knowledge concurrence and is not downgraded to invented merely for lack of a full source.

The exact witness x+x^2 psi(1/x) is a local composition with the bespoke oscillator. Its derivative at zero is 1 by direct division, while the recurring values psi'=3 and -3 force derivative values of opposite sign arbitrarily close to zero; the mean value theorem then rules out monotonicity on every neighbourhood.

This particular removable rational quotient is a locally selected worked example. Factoring x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1) and x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1) reduces the quotient to x off 1, and the derivative quotient independently tends to 1, so the claim is directly verified.

The exact counterexample is built from the bespoke periodic polynomial oscillator. With f(x)=x^2 psi(1/x) and g(x)=x, the quotient tends to zero by boundedness, but f'/g'=2x psi(1/x)-psi'(1/x) has two recurring subsequential limits. This directly refutes the converse without a literature-dependent step.

The source develops the Taylor polynomials for the geometric rational function and the geometric-series coefficients. The item records the finite exact algebraic remainder x^{n+1}/(1-x), valid for every x not equal to 1, rather than using a convergence claim.

The sources give the inconclusive zero-second-derivative warning and the higher-derivative test. The item packages the canonical x^4, -x^4, and x^3 witnesses and checks their derivatives and local order directly.

The source states the same orientation convention: reversing the endpoints negates the integral and an equal-endpoint integral is zero. The item only binds that standard convention to the library's Darboux integral.
The source states that Riemann integrability on [a,b] implies integrability on every closed subinterval, with the same hypotheses and direction. The Darboux-criterion proof in the item is local.

The sources state closure under scalar multiplication and addition and the identical linearity identity. The repository supplies a local upper/lower-sum proof. Its statement is correct; the separate step-reference typo in proof step 4.2 is recorded in the findings.
The sources state that pointwise f<=g for two Riemann-integrable functions implies the same order between their integrals. The item extends it to oriented notation by a direct local case split.

The sources give additivity for an ordered interior split and the subinterval integrability equivalence. The item packages the result for every third point and every endpoint order using the oriented-integral convention.
The source states that changing a bounded function at finitely many points preserves Riemann integrability and the integral. The item's oscillation-budget proof is local.

The peer-reviewed article states the same preservation theorem for a Riemann-integrable inner function and a continuous outer function on an interval containing its range. The item's uniform-continuity proof is local.

The sources give closure of Riemann-integrable functions under absolute value, products, maxima and minima. The item packages all four operations as one corollary and obtains the lattice formulas through continuous composition and algebraic identities.

The source states the broader weighted first mean value theorem for a one-signed integrable weight and places the witness in the open interval. The published item specializes to g >= 0, permits an endpoint witness, and gives a local proof with explicit zero-weight handling, so the source is semantic rather than verbatim support.
The sources define the variable-upper-limit integral function F(x)=integral_a^x f. The item merely fixes the same object in the library's oriented-integral notation.

The source proves that the integral function of a bounded Riemann-integrable function satisfies |F(x)-F(y)|<=M|x-y| and is continuous. The item's proof is the same mathematical estimate but was written locally from its integral bounds.

The sources state that the integral function of a Riemann-integrable f is differentiable at every point where f is continuous, with derivative f at that point. The repository adds explicit one-sided endpoint language already fixed by its derivative definition.

The sources state the Newton-Leibniz formula for a differentiable function whose derivative is Riemann integrable, with the same conclusion. The item's proof through the first FTC and constant-difference theorem is local.

The sources give existence of the integral-function primitive, uniqueness up to an additive constant, and evaluation of definite integrals by any primitive. The item collects these standard consequences in one corollary and applies its endpoint convention.

CMU Theorem 20 states the exact Riemann integration-by-parts theorem used here: differentiable u and v on [a,b], integrable derivatives, and the same boundary-term identity. The repository proof additionally makes integrability of the two products explicit.

The sources give change of variables for continuous f and a C^1 substitution. The item weakens C^1 to differentiability with Riemann-integrable derivative and uses the same oriented identity. Its proof through a primitive and the chain rule is local.

The source states Bonnet's second mean value formula for monotone g and integrable f, with the same endpoint coefficients and an intermediate xi, in the stronger Lebesgue setting. The item specializes it to bounded Riemann-integrable f and its oriented convention.
The sources state that a nonnegative continuous function on a compact interval with zero integral is identically zero. The item's positive-neighbourhood lower-bound proof is local.

The source states the integral test for a positive decreasing function and its sampled series. The item reformulates convergence of the improper integral as boundedness of the proper-integral sequence indexed from zero, allows nonincreasing nonnegative f, and records explicit comparison inequalities.

This is a repository-specific convention and scope record, including reading-order statements and deliberate omissions. Alpha checked every linked target on current disk and repaired the stale scaffold-era Taylor-integral-remainder assignment: the current Taylor page explicitly excludes that form, so the ledger now records it as absent with no published destination.

The university notes state exactly integral_0^1 x^m dx=1/(m+1) for nonnegative integer m. The item translates the integer into the library's canonical real embedding and supplies local FTC and consistency checks.

The particular two-level step function and its paired verification routes are a local worked construction. Splitting at 1 gives two constant integrals 1 and 3, and the displayed three-point Darboux partition gives matching sums after the single jump is isolated; the value 4 is directly verified.

The sources give the p-series threshold p>1 and the integral test. The item specializes to rational powers available in the library, indexes f_p(t)=(t+1)^{-p} from zero, and expresses improper convergence as boundedness of its proper-integral sequence. The mathematical threshold is sourced, but its last p=1 sentence falsely denies existence of a primitive and is proposed for repair.

The CLP university text computes (sqrt x)'=1/(2sqrt x) for x>0 and states that the derivative is undefined at zero; Active Calculus treats 1/sqrt x as an unbounded integrand at zero. The item scales by 2, proves the precise unbounded sequence, and packages those facts to explain why the proper Riemann FTC does not apply on [0,1].

The sources give the sign function's integral function as an absolute-value function and Darboux's theorem that derivatives cannot jump. The item packages these standard facts as an explicit refutation of the claim that every Riemann-integrable function has a primitive.

Olmsted's university-hosted differentiation counterexamples give the classical function x^2 sin(1/x^2), differentiable on a closed interval with an explicitly unbounded derivative. The published item names that classical witness and replaces its trigonometric oscillations by disjoint quartic bumps because trigonometric functions occur later in the library. The exact polynomial realization and its seam proof are local, but the mathematical counterexample is a recoverable source-backed alteration rather than an invented proposition.

The peer-reviewed source gives the same counterexample: Thomae's Riemann-integrable function composed with the integrable indicator of the positive range becomes Dirichlet's nonintegrable function. The repository's discontinuity-set verification is local.

The signed Dirichlet function, equal to 1 on rationals and -1 on irrationals, is a standard counterexample: its absolute value is constant while every Darboux lower and upper sum differs. Search located the exact witness only in non-qualifying discussion sources; reputable texts located during the pass state Dirichlet nonintegrability but not this full signed claim. It therefore requires Alpha's independent established-knowledge concurrence and is not mislabeled as invented.

The university notes give the standard moving/shrinking spike phenomenon: pointwise convergence to zero with every integral fixed at one. The item uses a specific continuous triangular tent supported on [0,1/(n+1)] and translates the construction into canonical-natural notation.

The locally selected witness f(t)=g(t)=t on [-1,1] directly refutes deletion of the one-sign hypothesis: integral g is zero while integral fg=integral t^2=2/3 is positive. Every computation follows immediately from the already cited polynomial integral and symmetry facts.

This exact undefinedness refutation is a bespoke composition of the preceding local quartic-bump function G with v(x)=x. The proof directly verifies that G is integrable while xG' remains unbounded at the displayed bump points, so one integral in the asserted equation does not denote.

Charles C. Pugh, Real Mathematical Analysis, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, Exercise 35(a)--(d), gives the same construction from a fat Cantor set F, psi(x)=integral_0^x dist(t,F) dt, nullity of psi(F), and the Riemann-integrable indicator of psi(F) whose composite with psi is not Riemann integrable. The Lehman College faculty-hosted full text exposes the exact exercise, while Springer supplies the canonical publisher record. The repository's quantitative content-zero proof and dependency-explicit packaging are local.

The source states the precise FTC continuity-point condition and gives the sign-function integral whose absolute-value cusp is not differentiable. The item combines that canonical witness with the standard finite-point-change witness to distinguish nonexistence of F' from existence with F' not equal to f.
